newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RESULTS TODAY - DEBT SEEN BURDENING STOCKS .
newsitem.headline: RESULTS TODAY - DEBT SEEN BURDENING STOCKS .

text.p: Steep finance charges, a much higher tax payment and a tough real estate market are expected to weigh down year earnings at South African hotels to building firm Stock and Stocks Ltd, analysts said.

They said the group's balance sheet gearing remained high, burdened by a large property portfolio which it had built up and not yet sold off. However, once these properties began moving Stocks was seen returning to robust earnings growth.

"Their cash requirements have gone up and up as they grew their property book and now they are sitting with big debt problems. They need to realise all these properties to pay off the debt," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.
"Once cashflows start turning around, then things will improve and the handcuffs will come off," he said, forecasting earnings growth of over 30 percent for the 1997/98 year.
Stocks earlier this year separately listed its hotels unit Stocks Hotels and Resorts Ltd in a move which analysts said was an attempt to reduce group debt levels.

Analysts polled by Reuters forecast Stocks' earnings per share for the year to end-April falling to between 57.0 and 63.0 cents a share with consensus at 61.0 cents -- a drop of 11.5 percent on the 69.0 cents earned a year ago.
They expected the dividend in a range of 11.0 to 15.0 cents with consensus at 14.0 cents compared to 15.0 cents last year.

Analysts said all property firms, including Stocks, were being pressured by tough market conditions mainly due to the country's high interest rates. The prime lending rate is at 20.25 percent although hopes for a cut soon are strong.

"Real estate is a tough place to be in. You've got high interest rates, a lot of people emigrating and the continuing feeling of uncertainty about the country's future is not conducive to property investments," an analyst said.
Stocks' rival Group Five Ltd last month said it would scale down its property development operations as a result of a depressed market.
Stocks' tax charge, which declined sharply last year helping the group to notch up a massive 60 percent increase in earnings, would return to normal levels again this year, analysts said.
Some losses in the group's information technology division and problems with its gaming operations in neighbouring Namibia were also seen weighing on profits.
